relationship: close narrative counterpart to Babylon's siege setting
rationale: The oracle is situated while Nebuchadnezzar and his forces fight Jerusalem and Judah's cities. The closing account dates Nebuchadnezzar's investment of Jerusalem and describes the siege lasting into Zedekiah's eleventh year; it supplies a particular counterpart for the Jerusalem part of that setting.

relationship: close threatened burning and subsequent account of Jerusalem's burning
rationale: The message to Zedekiah predicts that Babylon's king will seize and burn the city. The closing narrative records Nebuzaradan's arrival and the burning of the Lord's house, the royal house and the city's houses.

relationship: close repeated prediction of Zedekiah's encounter with Babylon's king
rationale: Both oracles deny Zedekiah's escape, describe his mouth and eyes meeting those of Babylon's king, and announce his entry into Babylon. The uncommon paired mouth-and-eye language makes the correspondence particularly close.

relationship: contrast between promised and denied royal lament
rationale: Zedekiah is promised mourning with the lament O lord. The oracle naming Jehoiakim denies mourning and the corresponding Alas, lord lament. The distinct kings receive opposite predictions about this public expression of royal honor.

relationship: related named fortified cities of Judah
rationale: Jeremiah identifies Lachish and Azekah among the fortified cities still resisting. Chronicles lists Lachis and Azeka among Rehoboam's walled and supplied cities. The passages give related fortification settings under different kings; their supplied spellings are preserved.

relationship: parallel solemn undertaking to end oppression within the community
rationale: Zedekiah concludes a covenant to proclaim release. Nehemiah's assembly promises restitution, swears before priests and carries out its undertaking. The comparison concerns a publicly pledged remedy for oppression; the later reversal in Jeremiah contrasts with Nehemiah's reported compliance.

relationship: close legal counterpart for freeing Hebrew male and female slaves
rationale: Jeremiah specifies release of both Hebrew male and female slaves. Deuteronomy explicitly provides for a Hebrew man or woman to serve six years and then be sent free; its stated service term is supplied by the law, rather than asserted in this individual source unit.

relationship: contrast between reversing and fulfilling an undertaking of restitution
rationale: The covenant participants turn back from their undertaking to release their slaves. Nehemiah records an oath of restitution and says the people carried out the word. The neighboring source unit explains the reversal as renewed enslavement.

relationship: parallel condemnation of enslaving fellow Judeans after release
rationale: The people thrust the released servants back into slavery. Nehemiah condemns selling Jewish brothers while he and his companions have been buying brothers out of foreign bondage. Both expose conduct that reverses liberation within the community.

relationship: close grounding of emancipation obligations in rescue from Egypt
rationale: The Lord recalls establishing the covenant when He rescued the fathers from Egypt's house of slavery. The emancipation law likewise grounds its command in Israel's former slavery and the Lord's redemption from Egypt.

relationship: close repetition of the six-year Hebrew-servant release law
rationale: The oracle states that the Hebrew brother serves six years and must be sent free when those years are complete. Deuteronomy gives the same service term and expressly names the seventh year as the time of release; Jeremiah adds the charge that the fathers did not obey.

relationship: parallel public covenant before the Lord at His house
rationale: Jeremiah recalls a covenant made before God in the house bearing His name. Kings describes a king and people at the Lord's house covenanting to uphold the written commandments. The commitments have different immediate contents, but share the public sanctuary setting and obligation before God.

relationship: related profanation of God's name through faithless solemn commitment
rationale: Reversing the promised release is explicitly called profaning God's name. Leviticus joins unjust swearing by that name with its profanation. Jeremiah concerns the covenant just made before God; the law addresses unjust use of His name in an oath.

relationship: close covenant judgment through sword, death and bread scarcity
rationale: The ironic proclamation of release hands the covenant breakers over to sword, death and famine. Leviticus describes the sword exacting the covenant's penalty, death among the people, surrender to enemies and scarcity of bread.

relationship: close covenant-curse language of scattering among earthly kingdoms
rationale: Jeremiah announces scattering among all the earth's kingdoms. Deuteronomy uses the same worldwide-kingdom scattering language in its curse of defeat before enemies, giving a specific counterpart to this part of Jeremiah's judgment.

relationship: close covenant curse of corpses feeding birds and beasts
rationale: Both passages consign the dead to the birds of heaven and beasts of the earth. Deuteronomy additionally says no one will drive the creatures away; Jeremiah applies the threat to the covenant breakers.

relationship: close threatened surrender and narrated capture of Zedekiah
rationale: The first clause promises to hand Zedekiah and the rulers to their enemies. The closing account describes Zedekiah's capture, judgment and removal to Babylon. This connection concerns that named royal surrender and does not resolve the source's unusual subsequent clause about the fleeing force.

relationship: close explanation of the returning force that will burn Jerusalem
rationale: The Lord promises to bring the force back to seize and burn the land's cities. The later oracle places the Chaldeans' withdrawal in the setting of Pharaoh's advance and then predicts their return to seize and burn Jerusalem.

relationship: related identification of Jonadab son of Rechab
rationale: The family names Jonadab son of Rechab as the father who commanded its abstinence. Kings independently names Jonadab son of Rechab meeting Jehu and joining his chariot. The target identifies the named figure without supplying the wine command itself.

relationship: related wine abstinence under different binding commitments
rationale: The Rechabites refuse wine because of their father's enduring command. Numbers requires abstinence from wine and vine products during a consecration vow. The comparison concerns commanded abstinence; it does not classify the Rechabites as the vow-takers described in Numbers.

relationship: parallel tent dwelling as sojourners in a land
rationale: The ancestral command requires tent dwelling rather than settled houses and cultivation in the land where the family spends its time. Hebrews describes Abraham living as a foreigner in the promised land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob. It does not impose the Rechabites' particular prohibitions on those patriarchs.

relationship: related obedience to a parental command
rationale: The descendants report that their entire households have kept Jonadab's command against wine. Colossians calls children to obey their parents in all things. Jeremiah gives an ancestral family practice; the letter states the household exhortation rather than that particular abstinence rule.

relationship: related parental obedience with a promise of life in the land
rationale: The family says it has obeyed and done everything its father commanded, including the tent dwelling previously connected with long life. Ephesians joins obedience and honoring parents with the promise of living long upon the earth.

relationship: related flight to Jerusalem before an invading force
rationale: The Rechabites explain their move into Jerusalem as escape from the Chaldean and Assyrian forces. Jeremiah's earlier warning calls people to gather into walled cities and flee to Zion before the northern calamity. The target supplies a comparable refuge response, without naming both forces in this source.

relationship: close refusal to hear and accept instruction
rationale: The question asks whether Judah and Jerusalem will accept discipline and hear God's words. The composite target describes the nation as neither hearing the Lord's voice nor accepting instruction, stating the same two failures directly.

relationship: parallel appeal from honor of a human father to honor due God
rationale: Jonadab's descendants keep his word while Judah refuses God's repeated speech. Malachi argues from a son's honor for his father to the honor God should receive as Father. Both use ordinary filial allegiance to expose failure toward God.

relationship: close repeated appeal to turn from evil and foreign gods
rationale: Both passages describe God sending His servants the prophets, calling each person to turn from evil practices, promising dwelling in the ancestral land and forbidding service to other gods. Their specific cluster of commands and assurances closely corresponds.

relationship: related contrast between obeying and failing a father's command
rationale: Jeremiah contrasts the Rechabites' obedience to their father with the people's failure to obey God. Jesus' two-child parable distinguishes the child who actually does the father's will from the one who does not. The target emphasizes action rather than an identical family or historical episode.

relationship: close judgment on Jerusalem after rejection of God's words
rationale: Both declarations bring upon Jerusalem the calamities previously spoken against it. The earlier courtyard oracle explicitly grounds the judgment in refusal to hear; the Rechabite comparison immediately supplies that refusal in the source's setting.

relationship: related honoring of obedience to parental instruction
rationale: The source grounds the following favorable promise in the descendants' obedience to their father's command. Proverbs urges attention to parental discipline and presents it as a crown and collar of honor. The rewards have different forms, while parental instruction is honored in both.

relationship: close promise that a family's man will not fail before God
rationale: The Rechabites receive a promise that a man of their family will not fail to stand before God. Solomon recalls the promise that a man of David's family will not be removed from before God on Israel's throne, subject to the stated obedience condition. The families and the royal office are distinct.

relationship: close shared fourth-year dating under Jehoiakim
rationale: Both introductions date a word to Jeremiah to the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. This is a precise chronological correspondence, without asserting that every word of the two literary settings was delivered on the same occasion.

relationship: parallel divine command to preserve prophetic words in writing
rationale: Jeremiah is told to put the delivered oracles on a writing roll. Isaiah is told to write on a tablet and in a book for enduring witness. The commanded written preservation is shared, while the specified media and scope differ.

relationship: close hope that hearing warning will bring repentance and mercy
rationale: Both passages use perhaps they will hear and turn from an evil way as the hoped-for response to a warning. The source speaks of mercy toward injustices and sins; the target speaks of ceasing from the planned calamities.

relationship: close corroborating notice of Baruch writing from Jeremiah's mouth
rationale: The source names Baruch son of Neriah writing the Lord's words from Jeremiah's mouth. The later notice again identifies Baruch writing words in the scroll from Jeremiah's mouth and dates the setting to Jehoiakim's fourth year.

relationship: related restriction of Jeremiah's movement by royal confinement
rationale: Jeremiah explains that being under guard prevents his entry into the Lord's house. The target describes Zedekiah shutting him in the royal prison court. These are distinct dated settings of the same prophet's confinement; the target does not identify the source's unspecified place of custody.

relationship: parallel public reading of sacred words in an assembly fasting before God
rationale: Baruch must read the roll publicly at the Lord's house on a fast day. Nehemiah describes an assembly fasting, confessing and reading God's law. The source is prophetic warning and the target is the law book, rather than the same document.

relationship: parallel prayer and turning from evil in hope of mercy
rationale: Jeremiah hopes an appeal for mercy and turning from evil will follow the reading amid threatened wrath. God's answer concerning the temple in Chronicles joins prayer, seeking Him and turning from wicked ways with forgiveness and healing of the land.

relationship: parallel reading a sacred document in the people's hearing
rationale: Baruch performs the instructed public reading of the Lord's words from the document. Nehemiah describes Esdras reading the law while the people's ears attend to it. Both identify the reader, written text and listening assembly.

relationship: parallel assembly of the people for a solemn fast
rationale: Jeremiah dates a gathering of Jerusalem and Judah for a fast before the Lord to Jehoiakim's eighth year and ninth month. Joel calls for a consecrated fast and gathered congregation. The target supplies no matching year or month.

relationship: close public reading of divine words at the Lord's house
rationale: Baruch reads Jeremiah's words in the Lord's house in all the people's hearing. Kings describes the king reading the covenant book to Judah, Jerusalem, priests, prophets and people at that house. The settings closely correspond while readers and documents differ.

relationship: parallel official report bringing a sacred document to royal attention
rationale: Micaiah reports to the rulers the words he heard Baruch read. Kings describes Sapphan bringing the book to Josiah, reporting its discovery and reading it before him. These are distinct stages of official transmission, not an assertion that the named messengers are the same person.

relationship: same-chapter contrast in reception of the prophetic roll
rationale: The rulers request that Baruch read the roll again to them. The king later cuts and burns it as Jehudi reads its columns. The two audiences' responses to the same written prophecy form a concrete literary contrast.

relationship: related named writers transmitting another speaker's message
rationale: Baruch identifies Jeremiah's oral report as what he wrote down. Tertius identifies himself as the writer of Romans, whose opening names Paul. The source expressly describes dictation; the target identifies the letter's writer without specifying that writing process.

relationship: parallel concealment of prophets threatened by royalty
rationale: The rulers tell Jeremiah and Baruch to hide and keep their whereabouts unknown. Kings describes Obadiah hiding the Lord's prophets when Jezebel was killing them. The particular common action is protective concealment under a royal threat.

relationship: parallel reading a recovered religious document before a king
rationale: Jehudi fetches the deposited roll and reads it to the king and the surrounding rulers. Sapphan reports the discovered law book and reads it before Josiah. Their different royal responses become explicit in the surrounding narratives.

relationship: same-chapter destruction of a scroll followed by its replacement
rationale: Jehoiakim cuts and burns the roll until it is consumed. The later command and fulfillment restore all its words in another roll, with additional words. The connection shows that destruction of the physical document does not end the announced message.

relationship: contrast between unresponsive and repentant royal hearing
rationale: Jehoiakim and his servants neither seek anything nor tear their garments upon hearing the words. Josiah tears his garments and orders inquiry of the Lord after hearing the law book. The comparison preserves the source's stated actions without substituting an unstated description of fear.

relationship: related royal rejection of warning counsel
rationale: The named rulers advise Jehoiakim not to burn the roll, against the burning already described. Amaziah rejects a prophet's counsel and is told that his refusal brings destruction. The advisers and the matters of counsel differ; the connection concerns disregarded royal warning.

relationship: parallel hidden prophetic servants escaping a royal threat
rationale: Jehoiakim orders Jeremiah and Baruch arrested, but they are hidden. Obadiah hides prophets during Jezebel's attacks. Jeremiah's unit does not name the agent of concealment, whereas Kings expressly names Obadiah.

relationship: parallel command to replace destroyed writing with its former words
rationale: Jeremiah is commanded to take another roll and write the words of the burned roll. Moses is commanded to prepare replacement tablets on which God will write the words of the shattered tablets. The media, writers and circumstances of destruction differ.

relationship: related prophecy of destruction affecting people and livestock
rationale: The king objects to the prediction that Babylon's king will destroy the land and that people and animals will cease from it. The target threatens death to the city's people and livestock, followed by the surrender of Zedekiah and the survivors. Both announcements concern Judah's judgment, with different immediate addressees and details.

relationship: close repeated judgment upon Jehoiakim's exposed corpse
rationale: Both named oracles against Jehoiakim predict his body being cast out dishonorably. Jeremiah 22 describes a donkey's burial beyond Jerusalem's gate; this source specifies exposure to daytime heat and nighttime frost.

relationship: close announced calamities following refusal to hear
rationale: The Lord will bring the previously pronounced calamities upon the king's circle, Jerusalem and Judah because they did not listen. The courtyard oracle likewise announces the spoken calamities upon Jerusalem and its surrounding settlements because they refuse God's words.

relationship: parallel writing after the loss of an earlier sacred document
rationale: Baruch writes the destroyed document's words again on another roll, with more words added. In the setting of replacement tablets, Exodus records writing the covenant's words. The comparison concerns renewed inscription; only Jeremiah explicitly mentions added words.

relationship: close appointment of Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar with differing succession notices
rationale: Both passages name Nebuchadnezzar as the one who made Zedekiah king over Judah. Jeremiah says he reigned in place of Jehoiakim, while the preceding Chronicles unit names Jechonias; the connection concerns the explicit appointment and does not harmonize that succession difference.

relationship: close refusal of Jeremiah's divine message under Zedekiah
rationale: Jeremiah says king, servants and people did not obey the Lord's words through the prophet. Chronicles says Zedekiah felt no shame before Jeremiah and God's word, then describes the officials', priests' and people's breaches of faith. Both connect the reign with rejection of the prophetic message.

relationship: close royal delegation seeking Jeremiah's intercession
rationale: Zedekiah sends men, including Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, asking Jeremiah to pray. The earlier delegation from the same king also includes that named priest and asks Jeremiah to inquire of the Lord concerning Babylon's attack. The other delegate's name differs.

relationship: related Egyptian military intervention and its inability to secure Judah
rationale: Pharaoh's advance causes a temporary Chaldean withdrawal in Jeremiah. Ezekiel describes the appeal to Egypt for military aid and denies a successful outcome for the covenant-breaking ruler. The target does not narrate this particular withdrawal, and the source does not claim lasting Egyptian deliverance.

relationship: parallel warning that Egyptian military help will fail
rationale: Jeremiah says the Egyptian force that came to help will return home. Isaiah rebukes reliance on Egypt's horses and chariots and says the helpers will grow weary. The common point is the failure of military confidence in Egypt, expressed through different predictions.

relationship: close repeated prediction of return, capture and burning
rationale: Both oracles say the force will return, take the city or land's cities and burn them. The source identifies the returning force as the Chaldeans; the earlier warning announces God's command bringing it back.

relationship: related rejection of false assurance about Jerusalem's safety
rationale: Jeremiah forbids assuming that the Chaldeans will depart for good. The temple sermon similarly warns against confidence in words promising benefit from the temple. The false assurances differ, but both concern unfounded confidence in Jerusalem's preservation.

relationship: related defeat by a seemingly insufficient force under divine judgment
rationale: Even pierced survivors of the Chaldean force are said to be capable of burning Jerusalem. Deuteronomy asks how one or two can rout multitudes unless God has delivered His people up. Neither target supplies the other's particular military numbers or injuries.

relationship: related purchase in Benjamin's land by Jeremiah
rationale: The source says Jeremiah leaves to buy from Benjamin's land. The field narrative names Anathoth in Benjamin and records his acquisition from Hanamel. The comparison identifies another explicit purchase involving the same prophet and district, without collapsing the distinct narrative settings into one event.

relationship: related accusation of political disloyalty met by denial
rationale: Sarouiah, the man with whom Jeremiah lodged, arrests him with the accusation of flight to the Chaldeans; Jeremiah denies it in the following unit. Nehemiah is accused of planning revolt and answers that the charge is fabricated. The allegations and accusers are different.

relationship: parallel explicit denial of an accusation of political disloyalty
rationale: Jeremiah calls the defection charge a lie and denies fleeing to the Chaldeans. Nehemiah denies the reported rebellion and says it was devised from the accuser's heart. Jeremiah additionally reports that his denial did not prevent arrest.

relationship: related episodes of Jeremiah being struck and confined
rationale: The rulers strike Jeremiah and put him into Jonathan's house as a prison. The earlier account describes Pashhur striking him and placing him in a trap at the Lord's house. The responsible authorities and forms of confinement remain distinct.

relationship: close repeated royal confrontation over the prediction of captivity
rationale: Zedekiah secretly asks whether there is a word from the Lord and receives the prediction of surrender to Babylon's king. The prison-court account likewise presents Zedekiah confronting Jeremiah over the oracle that city and king will be handed over and the king will enter Babylon.

relationship: parallel protest of confinement despite no wrong done
rationale: Jeremiah asks what wrong he has committed to warrant imprisonment. Joseph says he has done nothing yet has been cast into the pit. The source is a question to the king and the target an assertion to the cupbearer, not the same judicial episode.

relationship: related exposure of optimistic prophecy about Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah challenges the prophets who said Babylon's king would not come against the land. The target identifies Hananiah as a false prophet and records his promise that Babylon's yoke is smashed and deportees and vessels will return. These are distinct optimistic claims, not identical quoted predictions.

relationship: close later repetition of Jeremiah's prison appeal
rationale: Jeremiah asks not to be returned to Jonathan's house to die. In the later secret-interview narrative the king instructs him to report precisely that appeal. The target records the proposed report, while the source gives the appeal itself.

relationship: related provision of bread to prophets under threat
rationale: Jeremiah receives a daily loaf during confinement until the city's supply fails. Obadiah supplies hidden prophets with bread and water during Jezebel's attacks. The protectors and confinement settings differ, while food sustains endangered prophetic servants in both.

relationship: close repeated choice between remaining to die and surrendering to live
rationale: Both oracles say that remaining in the city brings death by sword and famine, while going out to the Chaldeans preserves life. The source calls life one's gain, while the target calls it spoil; both frame survival as what the surrendering person obtains.

relationship: close repeated prediction of the city's surrender to Babylon
rationale: Both declarations say Jerusalem will be handed over to Babylon's king. The target additionally specifies burning by fire and God's adverse purpose; those details are not added to this shorter source unit.

relationship: parallel accusation that a prophet's adverse words endanger the nation
rationale: Jeremiah's opponents tell the king that his words weaken fighters and people and deliver evil rather than peace. Amaziah tells Jeroboam that Amos conspires against him and that the land cannot endure his words of death and captivity. Both accusations portray unwelcome prophecy as a political danger.

relationship: parallel ruler yielding a prisoner's fate to hostile demand
rationale: Zedekiah puts Jeremiah in the accusers' hands; the account says the king was unable to oppose them. Luke describes the accusers' voices prevailing and Pilate handing Jesus over to their will. The rulers' stated motives and the resulting punishments differ.

relationship: close narrative parallel of being cast into a waterless pit
rationale: Jeremiah is lowered into a pit without water, where there is mire. Joseph is stripped and cast into an empty pit explicitly having no water. The shared waterless-pit confinement is specific; Genesis does not supply Jeremiah's mire.

relationship: close later divine address to the named Ethiopian rescuer
rationale: The source introduces Ebed-melech the Ethiopian as hearing of Jeremiah's confinement. The later oracle names the same Ethiopian and promises preservation amid the city's calamity because he trusted God. The intervening source narrative supplies his act of intervention.

relationship: related advocacy for a vulnerable person's just treatment
rationale: Ebed-melech confronts the king over the treatment that threatens Jeremiah with death from hunger. Proverbs calls for speaking, judging justly and deciding the case of the poor and weak. The comparison concerns intervention for a vulnerable person, without assigning Jeremiah a lifelong economic status.

relationship: parallel command to rescue someone facing death
rationale: The king orders Ebed-melech to bring Jeremiah out of the pit so that he does not die. Proverbs commands rescuing those led to death and ransoming those being killed. The source gives a particular intervention, including thirty men, rather than those details being supplied by the proverb.

relationship: close imagery of rescue from a pit and muddy confinement
rationale: Jeremiah is pulled out of the pit whose mire was described earlier. The psalm praises God for bringing the speaker out of a pit of misery and muddy slime. The source names a physical rescue by ropes; the comparison does not identify the psalmist with Jeremiah or the two passages as one event.

relationship: parallel demand that the recipient of a divine word conceal nothing
rationale: Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to hide no word from him. Eli similarly asks Samuel what was spoken and insists that no word be hidden; Samuel reports it all. The addressees and settings differ, while the demand for complete prophetic disclosure closely corresponds.

relationship: related danger of giving a king unwelcome prophecy
rationale: Jeremiah fears death if he answers and says the king will not heed counsel. Micaiah's adverse vision prompts the king's complaint that he prophesies only bad things. The surrounding target account later imprisons Micaiah; it does not say that the king kills him.

relationship: close royal oath by the living Lord not to kill a threatened servant
rationale: Zedekiah swears by the living Lord that he will not kill Jeremiah or hand him to the men. Saul likewise swears, As the Lord lives, that David will not die. The source additionally describes the Lord as the maker of their life.

relationship: close application of the surrender-and-life promise to the king
rationale: The source tells Zedekiah that going out to Babylon's commanders will preserve his life and household and prevent the city's burning. The earlier oracle offers life to anyone going out to the Chaldeans. Jeremiah here applies the same surrender condition to the king with further consequences for household and city.

relationship: close threatened surrender and burning of Jerusalem
rationale: The source warns that refusal to go out will leave the city to Chaldean capture and fire. The target likewise announces its handover to Babylon's king and burning. The source expressly frames that outcome against the preceding offered alternative.

relationship: related fear of people contrasted with trust in God
rationale: Zedekiah fears being handed to Judean deserters and mocked. Proverbs describes people being tripped up by fear and shame before others, contrasting them with the person who trusts in the Lord. The following source answer offers divine reassurance; the proverb does not name these deserters.

relationship: parallel contrast between hearing God for good and refusing Him unto harm
rationale: Jeremiah urges the king to hear the Lord's word so that it will be better for him and his life spared. Isaiah joins willing hearing with the land's good things and unwilling refusal with the sword. The immediate promised benefits differ, but the contrast of responses is shared.

relationship: close betrayal by those formerly described as peaceful allies
rationale: The women say the king's peaceful friends deceived him and will overpower him; they also describe those friends turning away. Obadiah says covenant allies and men at peace oppose and prevail over the addressee and set ambushes. Both expose trusted peaceful relationships becoming hostile; Obadiah does not use the source's slippery-feet wording.

relationship: close prediction and narrative counterpart of royal capture and city burning
rationale: The oracle predicts the king's seizure and Jerusalem's burning, alongside the removal of his household. The closing narrative records his capture and the subsequent burning of the houses. It gives additional details of his sons' deaths and his blinding rather than repeating the source's whole household prediction.

relationship: close prescribed report of an earlier prison appeal
rationale: The king tells Jeremiah to report his plea not to return to Jonathan's house to die. The earlier account records Jeremiah making that appeal. The source supplies what is to be told to the rulers, while the target contains the direct petition to the king.

relationship: close end of confinement followed by removal from the prison court
rationale: Jeremiah remains in the prison court until Jerusalem is taken. The subsequent account records his removal from that court and delivery to Gedaliah, after which he lives among the people. The connection traces the stated endpoint of his confinement without supplying an unstated exact release date.

relationship: close parallel dating of Nebuchadnezzar's siege
rationale: Both accounts place Nebuchadnezzar's arrival with his force against Jerusalem in Zedekiah's ninth year and tenth month. The closing account additionally supplies the tenth day and describes the enclosing works.

relationship: close parallel breach of Jerusalem at the siege's end
rationale: The source dates the breach to Zedekiah's eleventh year and the ninth day of the fourth month. The closing account gives the eleventh-year end of the siege, the ninth day and the breach, but does not repeat the fourth-month designation in those units.

relationship: related foreign rulers occupying Jerusalem's gates
rationale: The Babylonian commanders enter and sit at the Middle Gate. The opening oracle predicts northern kingdoms setting their thrones at Jerusalem's gate forecourts. The narrative supplies a particular gate occupation, without expressly calling the commanders' seats thrones.

relationship: close linked accounts of Jeremiah's release and residence with Gedaliah
rationale: The source records Jeremiah being removed from the prison court, handed to Gedaliah and living among the people. The next account describes release from handcuffs, permission to return to Gedaliah and residence with him at Mizpah. The distinct custody details are preserved rather than collapsed.

relationship: close identification of the Ethiopian addressed after rescuing Jeremiah
rationale: The oracle addresses Ebed-melech the Ethiopian in the setting of the city's coming calamity. The preceding chapter identifies him by the same name and origin and narrates his intervention to bring Jeremiah out of the pit. This supplies the recipient's particular narrative background.

relationship: related divine assurance of rescue to one who trusts
rationale: Ebed-melech is promised deliverance from the men he fears; the following source unit grounds the promise in his trust. The psalm promises rescue and presence in affliction to one who hopes in God. It is not an identification of the psalm's beneficiary with Ebed-melech.

relationship: close personal promises that preserved life will be one's gain
rationale: Both assurances promise life as gain amid announced calamity. This source addresses Ebed-melech and explicitly grounds rescue in trust; the later oracle addresses Baruch while warning him against seeking great things for himself.

relationship: related notices of Jeremiah being released from custody
rationale: The source introduces the chief guard's release of Jeremiah from handcuffs among the deportees. The preceding narrative records his removal from the prison court and placement with Gedaliah. The comparison concerns the named prophet's liberation and does not replace the native Daman wording with another place-name.

relationship: related acknowledgment of calamity previously announced against the city
rationale: The chief guard acknowledges that the Lord spoke the calamities against the place. Jeremiah's earlier oracle explicitly announces the city's surrender to Babylon's king and burning. The target supplies a specific earlier announcement rather than words quoted verbatim by the guard.

relationship: close explanation of national calamity as covenant disobedience
rationale: The guard says the Lord acted because the people sinned and did not obey His voice. Deuteronomy explains judgment on the land and removal to another land by abandonment of God's covenant and service to other gods. Both attribute the disaster to disobedience, with Deuteronomy specifying its idolatrous form.

relationship: close parallel appointment of a governor over Judah's remnant
rationale: Jeremiah's account names Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan as Babylon's king's appointee in Judah. Kings names Godolias son of Achikam son of Saphan in the same governing role over the people left in the land. The source additionally gives Jeremiah permission to live with him; the supplied name forms remain distinct in the quotations.

relationship: related residence and assembly at the governor's settlement
rationale: Jeremiah comes to Gedaliah at Mizpah and lives among those remaining. Kings describes the military commanders coming to Godolias at Massephath. The target supplies another gathering around the governor; it does not itself mention Jeremiah's residence.

relationship: close parallel report of the governor's appointment reaching the commanders
rationale: Both accounts describe Babylon's king appointing a governor over the remaining population and the commanders hearing of the appointment. Jeremiah additionally specifies the entrusted men and wives who had not been deported.

relationship: close parallel lists of commanders coming to the appointed governor
rationale: Both accounts list Ishmael, Johanan or Joanan, Seraiah or Saraias, and Jezaniah or Jezonias among those coming with their men to the governor. The supplied patronymics and the placement of the Netophathite description differ; the comparison does not make the lists identical.

relationship: close parallel oath urging settlement and service to Babylon's king
rationale: Both speeches reassure the commanders and their men concerning the Chaldeans and urge remaining in the land and serving Babylon's king for their good. Jeremiah says the Chaldeans' servants, whereas Kings says the passing of the Chaldeans; that wording difference is preserved.

relationship: related counsel to sustain settled life under Babylonian rule
rationale: Gedaliah tells the remnant to gather produce, store it and inhabit their towns while he stays at Mizpah. The letter to the deportees instructs building houses, planting gardens, eating their produce and seeking the land's peace. The source concerns Judah's remnant and the target the deportees, not one location.

relationship: related agricultural provision after displacement
rationale: Those returning to Gedaliah gather much wine, summer fruit and oil in Judah. The exiles' letter commands planting gardens and eating their fruit. The shared feature is settled provision from produce amid displacement; the target does not report this harvest or its abundance.

relationship: close warning of Ishmael's murderous intent followed by the attack
rationale: The commanders warn that Ishmael intends to take Gedaliah's life, although Gedaliah disbelieves them. The next chapter records Ishmael and his men attacking Gedaliah and those with him. It confirms the threatened attack without independently establishing the alleged commission from Ammon's king.

relationship: related anticipated danger to the gathered remnant and its later seizure
rationale: Johanan warns that Gedaliah's death would scatter the people gathered to him. The later narrative records Ishmael taking away the remaining people at Mizpah. This supports the particular danger to the settlement without endorsing Johanan's proposed preemptive killing or claiming it occurred.

relationship: close disbelief of a warning contradicted by the ensuing assault
rationale: Gedaliah calls Johanan's report about Ishmael false and forbids action against him. The ensuing account names Ishmael as the one who rises with his men and strikes Gedaliah. The narrative outcome directly bears on the disputed warning.

relationship: close parallel arrival of Ishmael with ten men in the seventh month
rationale: Both accounts place Ishmael's arrival with ten men and royal-family affiliation in the seventh month. Jeremiah names the grandfather Elasa and Kings Elisama; Jeremiah additionally records eating bread together. Those details are not silently harmonized.

relationship: related treachery in a relationship of shared bread
rationale: Ishmael eats bread with Gedaliah before the attack recorded next. The psalm laments treachery by a trusted man of peace who ate the speaker's loaves. The connection concerns betrayed table fellowship, not an identification of the psalmist or its unnamed companion.

relationship: close parallel attack by Ishmael and his ten companions on the governor
rationale: Both accounts describe Ishmael and ten men striking Babylon's appointed governor, named Gedaliah in Jeremiah and Godolias in Kings. Kings expressly adds that the governor died; the surrounding Jeremiah narrative likewise treats the attack as his killing.

relationship: close parallel inclusion of Judean and Chaldean victims
rationale: Jeremiah includes the Judeans with the governor at Mizpah and the Chaldeans found there among the victims. Kings likewise names Judeans and Chaldeans with the governor at Massephath. The shared victim groups are more specific than a general account of violence.

relationship: related grain offering accompanied by frankincense
rationale: The mourners carry grain offerings and frankincense to the Lord's house. Leviticus prescribes a flour offering with oil and frankincense, presented to the priests. The target explains the particular offering combination; it does not supply the source's eighty men or their mourning actions.

relationship: related invitation or private approach preceding concealed murderous intent
rationale: Ishmael invites the approaching mourners to Gedaliah although Gedaliah is already dead; the next unit records their slaughter. Joab has Abner brought back and draws him aside to speak while lying in wait, then strikes him. The invitations and victims differ, but deceptive approach precedes killing in both.

relationship: close illustration of wealth serving as ransom for life
rationale: Ten men disclose stores of grain, honey and oil, and Ishmael spares them. Proverbs says a man's own wealth is the ransom of his life. The narrative supplies a particular use of valuable provisions to avert death without approving the killer's conduct.

relationship: related Asa-Baasha conflict and Asa's construction at the remnant's settlement
rationale: Jeremiah attributes the large cistern to Asa because of Baasha. Chronicles narrates their conflict and Asa's subsequent building of Gabae and Maspha from Rama's materials. It supplies the named royal conflict and construction background but does not mention this cistern or establish its particular dimensions.

relationship: close realization of the warned danger to Gedaliah's gathered people
rationale: Ishmael takes away the people left at Mizpah, including the king's daughters. Johanan's earlier warning feared the scattering of the people gathered to Gedaliah after his death. The target anticipates the settlement's vulnerability rather than describing every detail of the later abduction.

relationship: related earlier warning by the commanders who later hear of the crimes
rationale: Johanan and his fellow commanders hear what Ishmael has done. The preceding account records their warning to Gedaliah and Johanan's attempt to prevent the threatened killing. The correspondence identifies their particular prior involvement, not merely another report of violence.

relationship: related military encounters beside Gibeon's water
rationale: Johanan's force finds Ishmael beside abundant water at Gibeon. Samuel locates the meeting of Abner's and Joab's forces at Gibeon's spring. These are distinct military encounters; Jeremiah does not specify that its abundant water is that same spring.

relationship: parallel recovery of people taken captive
rationale: The people taken with Ishmael return to Johanan. Samuel describes David recovering the people and possessions taken by the Amalekites. The common result is recovery from captivity; the source does not narrate David's method of battle or its spoils.

relationship: related flight to Ammon after an alleged Ammonite connection
rationale: Ishmael escapes to Ammon's people with eight men. The earlier warning alleges that Ammon's king sent him against Gedaliah. His destination is relevant to that allegation but is not independent proof of the king's commission.

relationship: parallel restoration of an abducted group including women
rationale: Johanan takes charge of the recovered people, including women, men and eunuchs. David recovers the captives, with his wives, sons and daughters expressly mentioned. The recovered groups are differently described; their lists and numbers are not equated.

relationship: close intended migration to Egypt followed by its narrated execution
rationale: The survivors stay near Bethlehem intending to enter Egypt. The later account records Johanan taking Judah's survivors into Egypt and reaching Taphnas. The target supplies the stated journey's outcome, not a different name for the source's stopping place.

relationship: close explanation of flight to Egypt after the governor's murder
rationale: Jeremiah says the survivors fear the Chaldeans because Ishmael killed Babylon's appointed governor. Kings places the governor's killing immediately before the people and commanders enter Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans. The same sequence of murder, fear and migration is explicit.

relationship: close communal request for a prophet's intercession amid danger
rationale: Judah's few survivors ask Jeremiah to pray to the Lord his God for them. Samuel's people similarly ask him to pray to the Lord his God so that they do not die. The requests share prophetic intercession for an endangered community, without identical circumstances or numbers.

relationship: close request that God disclose the way to follow
rationale: The people ask God to tell them the way they should go and what they should do. The psalm asks the Lord to make His ways known, teach His paths and guide the speaker in truth. One request concerns a community's immediate decision; the other is a personal prayer for guidance.

relationship: parallel commitment to report the whole divine word without concealment
rationale: Jeremiah promises to tell whatever the Lord answers and hide no word. Samuel reports all the words and hides nothing from Eli. The source is a prospective commitment; the target narrates its performance in a different prophetic setting.

relationship: parallel prophetic undertaking to pray for the people
rationale: Jeremiah agrees to pray to the Lord for those requesting intercession. Samuel declares that he must not cease praying for the people and will show them the good way. This target specifically supports the intercessory undertaking, distinct from the source's promise of complete disclosure.

relationship: parallel invocation of God as witness to a solemn undertaking
rationale: The people invoke the Lord as a righteous and faithful witness to their promise to act on His message. The covenant between Jacob and Laban explicitly invokes God as witness between them. Their obligations differ, but both place an undertaking before God's witness.

relationship: close public pledge to do and obey everything God speaks
rationale: The survivors promise to obey whether the answer is good or bad. At the covenant-book reading the people likewise promise to do and obey everything the Lord has spoken. The source makes the unconditional character of its pledged response especially explicit.

relationship: close contrast between pledged obedience and subsequent refusal
rationale: The people promise obedience to whatever divine answer comes. The ensuing narrative records named leaders rejecting Jeremiah's answer and the people refusing to remain in Judah. This gives the later outcome of the particular undertaking rather than a generic warning about disobedience.

relationship: close assurance of building and planting rather than destroying
rationale: Both promises use rebuilding without tearing down and planting without plucking out. The source conditions this assurance on the survivors remaining in the land; the earlier fig oracle concerns restoration of the deportees. The source's statement that God has rested from the calamities is not replaced with another expression.

relationship: close divine reassurance of presence and rescue against feared people
rationale: The survivors are told not to fear Babylon's king because God is with them to rescue and save them. Jeremiah's commission likewise says not to fear those addressed because God is with him to rescue him. The beneficiary and immediate threat differ.

relationship: related divine compassion and restoration
rationale: God promises mercy and return to the land. The psalm recalls His covenant mercy and granted compassion before captors, then asks for gathering from the nations. The source does not expressly make Babylon's king the agent of its promised mercy.

relationship: close warned refusal to remain followed by recorded disobedience
rationale: The oracle frames refusal to remain in the land as refusal to obey the Lord. The later narrative explicitly says Johanan, the commanders and the people did not obey by remaining in Judah. The target records the conduct anticipated in the warning.

relationship: parallel misplaced hope for security in Egypt
rationale: The survivors imagine Egypt as a place without war, trumpets or hunger. Isaiah warns that seeking Pharaoh's help and Egyptian shelter will bring shame and reproach. Isaiah says its people did not ask God; Jeremiah's people asked and then reject the answer, so their procedures are not equated.

relationship: parallel failure to escape danger by fleeing elsewhere
rationale: Sword and famine will meet the survivors in the Egypt to which they flee for safety. Amos pictures flight from a lion leading to a bear and apparent safety in a house ending in a snakebite. The source is a concrete destination warning, while the target expresses the futility of escape through images.

relationship: close repeated judgment upon those settling in Egypt
rationale: The source threatens those who set their faces toward Egypt with sword and famine. The later oracle likewise announces destruction of the Egyptian remnant through sword and famine, adding death in its comparison with Jerusalem. The source expressly includes foreigners as well as the people.

relationship: close comparison of Egypt's coming judgment with Jerusalem's
rationale: Both announcements apply to the emigrants in Egypt a judgment corresponding to what already struck Jerusalem. The source describes wrath and a resulting curse and reproach; the target names sword, famine and death.

relationship: close prohibition of entering Egypt and its subsequent violation
rationale: The Lord explicitly says not to enter Egypt. The later narrative says they entered Egypt because they had not obeyed His voice and identifies Taphnas as their destination. The target supplies the specific disobedience to this command.

relationship: related professed desire for God's word without doing it
rationale: Jeremiah condemns the people's request for prayer and promise to do the answer in light of their actual refusal. Ezekiel describes people eagerly gathering to hear a word from the Lord yet refusing to do it. Both distinguish an appearance of receptive listening from the response in action.

relationship: close charge of disobedience and its narrated form
rationale: Jeremiah says the people have not obeyed the voice with which the Lord sent him. The ensuing account identifies their disobedience as refusal to remain in Judah. The target specifies the action at issue in the source's accusation.

relationship: close repeated threat of death by sword and famine in Egypt
rationale: The source says the people will die by sword and famine in the place where they want to settle, identified as Egypt in the preceding warning. The later oracle explicitly names the remnant in Egypt and the same two instruments of death.

relationship: related challenge to an unwelcome prophet's divine authority
rationale: The leaders call Jeremiah's message a lie and deny that the Lord sent it. Zedekiah son of Chenaanah challenges what sort of the Lord's spirit spoke in Micaiah and strikes him. The forms of opposition differ, while both dispute the claimed divine source of adverse prophecy.

relationship: contrast between alleged influence and Baruch's recorded writing role
rationale: The leaders accuse Baruch of setting Jeremiah against them. The earlier account explicitly describes Baruch writing from Jeremiah's mouth the words God had delivered to the prophet. That recorded scribal role is relevant to the allegation without independently establishing every motive attributed to Baruch here.

relationship: close refusal of the specific command against entering Egypt
rationale: The narrative says the commanders and people did not obey by remaining in Judah. The preceding oracle expressly forbids the survivors to enter Egypt. This is the particular divine instruction against which the conduct is measured.

relationship: related movement of the survivors who had returned to Judah
rationale: Johanan takes the survivors who had returned to live in the land. The earlier account describes Judeans returning from neighboring countries to Gedaliah in Judah. It supplies the preceding return movement without asserting that its list identifies every individual now departing.

relationship: close identification of the population entrusted to Gedaliah
rationale: Both passages name the king's daughters and the people entrusted by the chief guard to Gedaliah. The source also explicitly includes Jeremiah and Baruch; the target does not name those two among Ishmael's captives.

relationship: close parallel account of the survivors' entry into Egypt
rationale: Both narratives describe the people and military commanders entering Egypt after the governor's murder. Kings expressly gives fear of the Chaldeans; Jeremiah stresses disobedience to God's voice and names Taphnas. The stated explanations are preserved rather than substituted for each other.

relationship: related Egyptian oracle settings at Taphnas and Tahpanhes
rationale: Jeremiah receives the word at Taphnas that introduces the following sign of Babylonian domination. Ezekiel names Tahpanhes in an oracle of Egypt's shattered power and captivity. The distinct supplied place-name forms are preserved, and the source introduction is not made to contain Ezekiel's darkness imagery.

relationship: parallel public material sign interpreted as coming judgment
rationale: Jeremiah is told to hide stones before the Judeans' eyes, with their meaning stated in the next unit. The earlier command breaks a jar before accompanying men and explains it as the people's and city's breaking. The prophetic method is shared; the objects and predicted actions differ.

relationship: close prophecy that Nebuchadnezzar will receive Egypt
rationale: Jeremiah announces Nebuchadnezzar's arrival and throne above the hidden stones in Egypt. Ezekiel likewise names Nebuchadnezzar as the recipient of Egypt from God, there as wages for his force. The target does not mention Jeremiah's stones or throne-sign.

relationship: close formula assigning people to death, sword or captivity
rationale: Both declarations distribute people to their appointed forms of judgment using the repeated construction those for a fate, to that fate. Jeremiah 15 includes famine as well; the source names death, deportation and sword in its Egyptian setting.

relationship: related judgment upon Egypt's gods in different historical settings
rationale: The source predicts burning the gods' houses and deporting the gods during the Babylonian attack. Exodus announces the Lord's vengeance upon Egypt's gods in the Passover setting. The agents, actions and occasions differ; both specifically include Egyptian deities within judgment.

relationship: related humiliation of deities carried into captivity
rationale: Jeremiah's oracle includes the deportation of Egypt's gods. Isaiah depicts the images of Bel and Dagon as burdens and says they themselves were led captive. This connection concerns divine images' captivity and does not identify those named images with the source's Egyptian gods or reinterpret its delousing simile.

relationship: related destruction of cultic pillars and shrines
rationale: Jeremiah predicts the shattering of the City of the Sun's pillars and burning of the houses. Exodus commands the breaking of pillars and destruction of other cultic objects in the land Israel is entering. This is a comparison of destructive treatment of rival cults, not an assertion that the commands describe the same place or army.

relationship: related setting of Judean survivors in Egyptian Taphnas
rationale: The oracle addresses Judean communities in Egypt, including Taphnas. The preceding narrative records Johanan's party entering Egypt and reaching Taphnas. The target accounts for one stated destination without placing all the source's other communities there.

relationship: close recollection of Jerusalem's desolation after captivity
rationale: Jeremiah points to the devastation and emptied cities already visible in Judah. Lamentations opens with Israel taken captive, Jerusalem laid waste and the once populous city sitting alone. The lament specifically supports the Jerusalem portion of the source's wider judgment on Judah's cities.

relationship: close provocation through worship of previously unknown gods
rationale: The source attributes the calamity to provoking God by incense to other gods whom the people did not know. Deuteronomy speaks of provocation by foreign gods and sacrifice to gods they did not know. The forms of ritual action differ, while the unknown foreign recipients and divine provocation correspond.

relationship: close repeated sending of God's prophetic servants from dawn
rationale: Both passages describe God sending His servants the prophets at dawn. This source adds the particular prohibition of the hated act of defilement; the target places the repeated sending across the period since the exodus.

relationship: parallel rejection of repeatedly sent divine messengers
rationale: Jeremiah says the people did not listen or turn from incense to other gods. Chronicles describes God's repeated sending of prophets and the people's disregard of His words and mockery of His messengers. The source specifies the ritual practice from which they refused to turn.

relationship: related divine wrath and destructive fire
rationale: Jeremiah says wrath dripped out and blazed in Judah's cities and outside Jerusalem. Lamentations describes poured-out fury and fire kindled in Zion consuming her foundations. The shared wrath-and-fire imagery connects the city's destruction with divine judgment.

relationship: close rhetorical charge that idolatrous provocation harms the people themselves
rationale: The source asks why the people do great evils against themselves, cutting off their households. The earlier oracle asks whether their provocative worship harms God or themselves to their shame. Both turn attention from the purported benefit of the cult to the worshipers' own harm.

relationship: close warning against provoking God through service to foreign gods
rationale: The source connects the works of their hands and incense to other gods with their own cutting off and reproach. Jeremiah 25 forbids service and worship of foreign gods so as not to provoke God through their hands' works into harming them. Neither comparison requires treating every mention of hands' works as an expressly described manufactured statue.

relationship: related warning not to repeat the fathers' evil
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether the earlier generations' and rulers' evils have been forgotten. Zechariah recalls God's anger with the fathers and forbids becoming like those who ignored calls to turn from evil. The source includes wives and rulers in addition to the fathers.

relationship: close failure to heed the ordinances given to the fathers
rationale: The source says the people have not stopped their practices or held fast to the ordinances set before the fathers. The earlier passage recalls the command to hear and walk in God's ways and the fathers' refusal. Both describe persistence in the opposite course to the received command.

relationship: related image of God setting His face in destructive judgment
rationale: The source states only that God is setting His face; its following unit supplies destruction of the Egyptian remnant. Leviticus explicitly sets God's face against a man and his kin in judgment. The connection concerns this image of divine opposition, not an identification of the different offenses.

relationship: close repetition of sword and famine against the Egyptian remnant
rationale: Both oracles locate the threatened people in Egypt and announce death by sword and famine. The source emphasizes the least and greatest and the resulting reproach and curse, while the earlier warning emphasizes the failure of the hoped-for escape.

relationship: close parallel between judgment in Egypt and prior judgment in Jerusalem
rationale: The source expressly says Egypt's residents will be visited as Jerusalem was. The earlier warning likewise compares wrath on those entering Egypt with wrath already falling on Jerusalem. Their lists of the judgment's effects differ.

relationship: same-chapter clarification of the exception for rescued returnees
rationale: The source denies return to Judah except for those rescued. The later statement identifies sword survivors who return, few in number. This clarifies the expressly stated exception rather than changing the warning into a promise of universal return.

relationship: same-chapter link between men's knowledge and the women's appeal to their husbands
rationale: The source identifies men who knew of their wives' incense alongside the answering women. The women's later question asks whether they made cakes and poured offerings without their husbands. These statements connect the household participants without making mere knowledge identical to each person's performance of every ritual.

relationship: close explicit refusal to hear the divine warning
rationale: The people directly refuse to listen to Jeremiah's word in the Lord's name. In the earlier oracle they likewise answer the call to hear the watchers' trumpet by saying they will not hear. Both record an open verbal refusal rather than inadvertent failure to understand.

relationship: related false attribution of material well-being to rival objects of devotion
rationale: The speakers credit devotion to the queen of heaven with bread and prosperity. Hosea's woman credits her lovers with provisions, while God says He gave the grain, wine and oil that she failed to recognize. The rival recipients differ; the comparison does not identify the queen of heaven with Baal or the lovers.

relationship: contrast between rival explanations of lost provision
rationale: The people claim that stopping incense to the queen caused scarcity, sword and famine. Hosea identifies God as the provider who takes back His grain and wine. The target supplies a contrasting account of deprivation, while Jeremiah's subsequent reply likewise rejects the speakers' defense of their cult.

relationship: close household involvement in cakes and drink offerings to heavenly recipients
rationale: The women mention making cakes and pouring drink offerings and question whether this was without their husbands. The earlier oracle describes children, fathers and women preparing cakes for heaven's host and pouring offerings to foreign gods. The source says queen of heaven, whereas the target says heaven's host; the recipients' terms are not made identical.

relationship: related divine remembrance of cultic wrongdoing for judgment
rationale: Jeremiah says the people's earlier incense came into God's heart and remembrance. Hosea says God does not accept the sacrifices and will remember injustices and punish sins. Both oppose a favorable reading of ritual conduct by invoking God's adverse remembrance.

relationship: close correspondence between covenant curses and the desolate land
rationale: Jeremiah explains the land's desolation and curse by unbearable wickedness and abominations. Leviticus threatens desolate cities and land, ruined holy places and scattering among nations for covenant disobedience. The source describes the resulting condition; the target states the threatened consequences.

relationship: close causal link between refusing God's voice and overtaking calamities
rationale: The source attributes the calamities to failing to obey God's voice and walk in His ordinances, law and testimonies. Deuteronomy says curses will come and overtake those who do not hear the Lord's voice and keep His commandments. The source also specifies the incense that occasioned the charge.

relationship: contrast between fulfillment of idolatrous pledges and vows made to God
rationale: The source says the women carried out their pledges to the queen of heaven. Ecclesiastes requires paying vows made to God and warns against vowing without paying. The comparison concerns the seriousness of enacted pledges while distinguishing their recipients; it does not commend the women's idolatrous vows.

relationship: related withholding of the Lord's name amid judgment
rationale: The source announces that Judeans in Egypt will no longer invoke the living Lord's name. In Amos, amid deaths in a house, one person tells another to be silent so as not to name the Lord. The source is God's sworn declaration; the target records a human warning, not that identical oath.

relationship: related divine oath by God's own authority
rationale: God swears by His great name in the source. Hebrews says God swore by Himself because there was no greater by whom to swear. The oath in Hebrews confirms blessing to Abraham, while Jeremiah's oath announces judgment.

relationship: close divine attention directed toward harm rather than good
rationale: Jeremiah says God watches the people for harm, not good, and announces sword and famine. Amos says God will fix His eyes on the captives for evils, not good things, and command the sword against them. The correspondence concerns purposeful divine attention in judgment.

relationship: related testing of disputed words by their eventual outcome
rationale: The few returnees will learn whose word endures, after rival claims about safety and prosperity. Deuteronomy judges a claimed divine word by whether it comes to pass. The source's disputed speakers are not all described as prophets, whereas the law addresses prophetic claims explicitly.

relationship: close narrative counterpart to the stated Zedekiah comparison
rationale: The threat against Egypt's Ouaphre is compared with God's handover of Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar. The closing narrative records Zedekiah's capture and removal to Babylon. It supports the named comparison, without supplying a narrated fulfillment of Ouaphre's fate.

relationship: close corroborating notice of Baruch's writing in Jehoiakim's fourth year
rationale: Both accounts place Baruch's writing from Jeremiah's mouth in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah. The earlier narrative describes the commission and act; this source introduces the personal word addressed to the writer.

relationship: close lament of weary groaning at one's resting place
rationale: Baruch says he lay amid groanings and found no rest after toil was added to pain. The psalm speaks of weariness with groaning and tears wetting the bed and resting place. It supplies a comparable bodily lament, not Baruch's identity or the same occasion.

relationship: close opposing images of uprooting or demolishing and building or planting
rationale: God announces tearing down what He built and plucking up what He planted. Jeremiah's commission similarly includes uprooting and demolishing alongside building and planting. The source describes reversal of prior constructive work, while the commission lists the prophet's appointed scope.

relationship: close personal assurance that one's life will be gain amid calamity
rationale: Baruch is promised his life as gain wherever he goes while calamity comes upon all flesh. Ebed-melech likewise receives a promise that his life will be his gain. Their immediate grounds differ: Baruch is warned against seeking great things, while Ebed-melech is commended for trust.

relationship: parallel refusal to pursue great things for oneself
rationale: The source forbids Baruch to seek great things for himself amid general calamity. The psalm says the speaker's heart and eyes are not exalted and that he has not walked among great things beyond him. This target supports the restraint of ambition, distinct from the source's promise of preserved life.

relationship: close parallel age and length of Zedekiah's reign
rationale: Both accounts state that Zedekiah began to reign at twenty-one and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. The source additionally names his mother and adds Lobena, details which this target does not provide.

relationship: close parallel regnal notice including the king's mother
rationale: Both notices give the age twenty-one and eleven years in Jerusalem and name the mother as a daughter of Jeremiah. The source says Zedekiah and Amitaal and adds Lobena; Kings says Sedekias and Amital and does not name Lobena in this unit.

relationship: close parallel commencement of the Babylonian siege
rationale: Both place the Babylonian king's arrival with his force in the ninth regnal year and tenth month and describe surrounding siegeworks. Jeremiah adds the tenth day and specifies a palisade and squared stones; Kings describes an enclosing wall.

relationship: close parallel endpoint of the siege
rationale: Both accounts say the city remained besieged until the king's eleventh year, naming him Zedekiah in Jeremiah and Sedekias in Kings. Neither comparison changes the supplied chronology or name forms.

relationship: close parallel report of famine and absence of bread
rationale: Both accounts place severe famine on the ninth of the month and say there were no loaves for the people of the land. The individual units do not themselves supply the month's number.

relationship: close parallel escape route after Jerusalem's breach
rationale: Both describe the breach, warriors going out at night by the gate between walls beside the king's garden, the surrounding Chaldeans and the route toward Arabah or Araba. The detailed cluster supports a close narrative comparison without normalizing the place-name forms.

relationship: close parallel pursuit and capture near Jericho
rationale: Both describe the Chaldean pursuit overtaking the king near Jericho and the dispersal of those with him. Jeremiah calls them his servants; Kings calls them his force. The corresponding movement is shared without making those designations identical.

relationship: close parallel royal judgment at Deblatha
rationale: Both accounts bring the captured king to Babylon's king at Deblatha and describe judgment being spoken upon him. The named place and judicial encounter provide a specific counterpart.

relationship: close parallel killing of the king's sons before his eyes
rationale: Both accounts explicitly put the sons' slaughter before the father's eyes. Jeremiah additionally reports the killing of Judah's rulers at Deblatha; Kings proceeds to the king's blinding and fetters.

relationship: close parallel blinding, fetters and deportation of the king
rationale: Both accounts describe the king being blinded, bound with fetters and brought to Babylon. Jeremiah additionally places him in a mill house until death; that detail is not replaced with a conventional prison description or attributed to Kings.

relationship: related prediction of arrival in Babylon without seeing it
rationale: Jeremiah's blinded king is brought to Babylon. Ezekiel predicts that Jerusalem's ruler will be caught, brought to Babylon and not see it, and die there. The narrative supplies a particular counterpart to arrival without sight; Ezekiel does not name Zedekiah in the target unit.

relationship: close parallel arrival of the Babylonian officer with a differing day
rationale: Both accounts place the officer's arrival at Jerusalem in the fifth month. Jeremiah gives the tenth day and calls him chief guard; Kings gives the seventh day, the nineteenth year of the Babylonian king, and the title chief cook. The differing details remain explicit.

relationship: close parallel burning of the sanctuary, palace and city houses
rationale: Both accounts name the Lord's house, the king's house and Jerusalem's houses as burned. The target's final agent phrase continues into verse10, so both actual units are retained together as one passage.

relationship: close parallel demolition of Jerusalem's wall
rationale: Jeremiah records the Chaldean force pulling down Jerusalem's wall all around. Chronicles likewise says the wall was demolished amid the burning of the sanctuary and citadels. This target expressly contains wall demolition, unlike the supplied 2 Kings 25:10 wording.

relationship: close parallel retention of people as vinedressers
rationale: Both accounts say the Babylonian officer left people as vinedressers. Jeremiah adds farmers; Kings calls the remaining people poor and adds the native term gabin. The comparison does not silently translate that latter term as the source's farmers.

relationship: close parallel removal of bronze temple fixtures to Babylon
rationale: Both accounts describe Chaldeans shattering the bronze pillars and Sea and carrying their bronze to Babylon. Jeremiah names bases, whereas Kings retains mechonoth. The shared named fixtures and destination are explicit without replacing that native term.

relationship: parallel inventories of bronze service utensils with differing item lists
rationale: Both passages enumerate bronze objects used in service, including bowls. Jeremiah also names the rim and meat forks; Kings names cauldrons, iamin and incense dishes. The inventories are related without treating all the supplied item names as interchangeable.

relationship: close parallel taking of gold and silver temple vessels
rationale: Jeremiah distinguishes the gold and silver objects taken by the chief guard within a broader utensil list. Kings records the chief cook taking firepans and gold and silver bowls. This supports the precious-metal spoliation without supplying glosses for saphphoth or masmaroth.

relationship: close parallel unweighed bronze of Solomon's temple furnishings
rationale: Both accounts name Solomon, two pillars, one Sea and bronze beyond a reckoned weight. Jeremiah includes twelve calves beneath the Sea, while Kings includes mechonoth. Their lists are not made identical.

relationship: close counterpart for twelve animals supporting the Sea
rationale: Jeremiah names twelve bronze calves beneath the Sea. Kings describes twelve cattle beneath it, grouped three in each of four directions, with the Sea above them. This target specifically supports the supporting-animal arrangement rather than the separate unweighed-bronze statement.

relationship: parallel descriptions of a temple pillar with differing heights
rationale: Jeremiah assigns one pillar a height of thirty-five cubits; Kings gives one pillar eighteen cubits. Both describe the same class of temple furnishing, but the measurements are expressly different and are not reconciled by the comparison.

relationship: related thirty-five-cubit pillar description with different grammatical scope
rationale: Jeremiah describes one pillar as thirty-five cubits high. Chronicles describes two pillars before the house as thirty-five cubits in height. The shared measurement language is noted without deciding whether the latter expression measures each pillar or combines them.

relationship: close correspondence of pillar ornaments, nets and pomegranates
rationale: Jeremiah describes bronze cornices surrounded by netting and pomegranates. Kings lists pillar ornaments covered by nets and rows of pomegranates. The differing ornament terminology and the target's four-hundred enumeration are preserved rather than made identical to Jeremiah's count.

relationship: related hundred-pomegranate enumeration with differing descriptions
rationale: Jeremiah counts ninety-six on one side and one hundred around the net. Chronicles says a hundred pomegranates were made and placed on hanging ornaments. The passages share a numbered pomegranate decoration but do not explain how their arrangements and counting scopes correspond.

relationship: parallel seizure of priestly personnel and three guards with different identifications
rationale: Both accounts include a first priest and three guards in the seized group. Jeremiah leaves the priests unnamed and calls the guards men guarding the road; Kings names Saraias and Sophonias and calls the three doorpost guards. The comparison does not identify the unnamed second priest with a named person or erase the different guard descriptions.

relationship: close parallel captive officials with a differing court-party count
rationale: Both lists include a eunuch supervising warriors, a military scribe and sixty people found in the city. Jeremiah gives seven prominent men in the king's presence; Kings gives five who saw his face. That numerical difference is retained.

relationship: close parallel transfer of captives to Babylon's king at Deblatha
rationale: Both accounts describe the Babylonian officer taking the detained group to the king at Deblatha. Their supplied officer titles differ, chief guard in Jeremiah and chief cook in Kings.

relationship: close parallel royal violence at Deblatha in Aimath
rationale: Both accounts say Babylon's king struck the captives at Deblatha in Aimath's land. Kings explicitly adds that he put them to death and that Judah was deported; the source's shorter wording is preserved.

relationship: close parallel royal release with differing day and name forms
rationale: Both date a Judean king's release to the thirty-seventh year of deportation and the twelfth month. Jeremiah names Ioakim and gives the twenty-fourth day; Kings names Joakim and gives the twenty-seventh. The close sequence is compared without harmonizing those details or supplying a different Judean royal name.

relationship: close parallel kind speech and elevation above other kings
rationale: Both passages describe kind speech to the Judean king and placement of his throne above those of the other kings in Babylon. The distinct supplied names in their preceding units remain as written.

relationship: close parallel change of prison clothing and continual royal meals
rationale: Both accounts describe changing prison garments and eating bread continually before the Babylonian king throughout life. The clothing and daily-table details form a specific verbal and narrative correspondence.

relationship: close parallel daily royal allowance for life
rationale: Both accounts give continual provision from the Babylonian royal establishment, apportioned day by day for the rest of the Judean king's life. Jeremiah calls it an allowance and expressly says until death; Kings describes table provision and each day's portion.
